rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A projectile runs two independent motions on one clock: uniform horizontal velocity $u\cos\theta$ and vertical free fall from $u\sin\theta$. For an angled launch on level ground, the time of flight is $T = 2u\sin\theta/g$ (exactly twice the time to the top — NEB 2019), the maximum height is $H = u^2\sin^2\theta/2g$, and the range is $R = u^2\sin2\theta/g$ — maximal at 45° and identical for complementary angles, so…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - uₓ = u cos θ; u_y = u sin θ - T = 2u sin θ/g; H = u² sin²θ/2g; R = u² sin 2θ/g - Horizontal projection: t = √(2h/g); R = u√(2h/g); v = √(u² + 2gh) - Trajectory: y = x tan θ − gx²/(2u² cos²θ)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Independence of Components:** Horizontal motion (constant $v_x = u\cos heta$) and vertical motion (free fall $v_y = u\sin heta - gt$) are completely independent. They share only the time variable $t$. This is the foundational principle — no horizontal force means $v_x$ is constant.  ·  **Trajectory is a Parabola:** Eliminating $t$ gives $y = x an heta - rac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2 heta}$, a downward-opening parabola. This assumes no air resistance, constant $g$, and flat ground. With drag, the trajectory is not a parabola and range decreases.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Note 1: In horizontal-launch problems, get the time from the VERTICAL fall first, then multiply by $v_x$.  ·  Note 2: Memorise $\sin 37° = 0.6$, $\cos 37° = 0.8$ and $\sin 2\theta$ values for 30°/45°/60° — NEB numericals use them constantly.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **Angle projection vs horizontal projection:** angled launch uses T = 2u sinθ/g; horizontal launch from a height uses t = √(2h/g) — different formulas for different setups.  ·  **Maximum range at 45°:** true only for level ground (launch and landing at the same height).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Task 1: Derive $T$, $H$, $R$ from components in writing, then specialise to $\theta = 45°$.  ·  Task 2: Solve ten numericals: horizontal launches, angled launches, and velocity-at-time/height cases.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): Find the maximum range of a projectile launched at 40 m/s on level ground.** — R_max = u²/g at 45° = 1600/10 = 160 m (g = 10 m/s²).

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Most-tested unit so far: five verified questions. Practise all three setups (angled, horizontal, vertical) and both derivations.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Independence again:** the horizontal motion never knows about gravity; the vertical motion never knows about u cos θ — one clock, two independent problems.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Components: u cos θ constant horizontal; u sin θ vertical under g.  ·  T = 2u sinθ/g; H = u²sin²θ/2g; R = u²sin2θ/g; R max at 45°.  ·  Complementary angles (θ, 90°−θ) give equal ranges — 30° and 60° ratio 1:1.  ·  Horizontal projection: t = √(2h/g), R = ut, v = √(u² + 2gh).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Without air resistance a bullet fired horizontally and a bullet dropped from the same height hit the ground at the same instant.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Two Motions Wearing One Body A projectile is free fall with a head start: uniform horizontal velocity (a = 0) superposed on vertical free fall (a = g). Because the components are independent, the whole parabolic story unfolds from two one-dimensional problems sharing one clock.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Projectile launched at angle θ with speed u (level ground) | Quantity | Formula | |---|---| | Horizontal component | $u_x = u\cos\theta$ (constant throughout) | | Vertical component | $u_y = u\sin\theta$ (changes by g) | | Time to maximum height | $t_{up} = u\sin\theta/g$ | | **Time of flight** | $T = 2u\sin\theta/g$ | | **Maximum height** |…  ·  ## 3. Worked Numericals **Q1 (3m, 2024):** A body is projected with velocity 20 m/s at 30° to the horizontal. Find its maximum height and horizontal range. (g = 10 m/s²) *Given:* u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°. *Substitution:* $H = u^2\sin^2\theta/2g = 400 \times 0.25/20 = 5$ m. $R = u^2\sin2\theta/g = 400 \times \sin60°/10 = 40 \times 0.866 = 34.6$ m.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Symmetry and Range Maxima:** Time of flight $T = rac{2u\sin heta}{g}$, max height $H = rac{u^2\sin^2 heta}{2g}$, range $R = rac{u^2\sin 2 heta}{g}$. Maximum range at $ heta = 45^\circ$. Complementary angles ($ heta$ and $90^\circ- heta$) give identical ranges because $\sin 2 heta = \sin(180^\circ-2 heta)$.…  ·  Note 3: 'Same range' pairs: compare heights as $\sin^2\theta : \sin^2(90°-\theta)$ — the steeper shot rises 3× higher for the 30°/60° pair.  ·  Note 4: State the assumptions (no air resistance, constant $g$, flat ground) in theory answers — they define the model.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Verified PYQs: 2024 numerical 3m; 2022 complementary-angles derivation 3m; 2022 horizontal-projection 5m; 2022 vertical projection 4m; 2019 T = 2·t_up derivation 3m.  ·  "A projectile writes a parabola because one axis coasts while the other falls."  ·  Why do 30° and 60° give the same range but different maximum heights?
